title: The new BJP team’s piecemeal reset
author: Nistula Hebbar
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi walked into a meeting of the newly appointed Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national office-bearers on August 22. The 64 office-bearers present assumed he would address them on how they should approach their assignments. Instead, he spent the next four-and-a-quarter hours individually querying them on their past organisational work.

The exchange was unhurried, with PM Modi at one point telling the audience that he too was once like them, a national office-bearer of the party during the late Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s tenure as Prime Minister (1999-2004), say some of the new office-bearers.

The identification was interpreted in some quarters as a pep talk to the new team of how far organisational service can take you in the BJP, but for others it pointed to a unifying characteristic in a list of names that otherwise lacked a meta narrative, and instead, in a piecemeal fashion exhibited the political anxieties of the BJP.

This privileging of organisational experience by the Prime Minister was the highlight of the new team. The BJP, now in its third term in power and seeking a fourth in 2029, is, with this new team, attempting a reset amid various political anxieties.

Journalist Shekhar Iyer, who has tracked the BJP for decades, says, “The new team marks a big shift in the party top brass’ approach to the challenges ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha poll. Increasingly, the BJP is signalling to itself that, henceforth, the chosen men and women will represent less of their individual personality and more of their abilities and capabilities for the tasks to be accomplished.”

“The BJP is signalling to itself that, henceforth, the chosen men and women will represent less of their individual personality and more of their abilities and capabilities for the tasks to be accomplished”Shekhar IyerJournalist

This means the BJP is choosing workers over personalities, some of whom may not be known to the world outside the party. “If they meet the expectations of the top brass, they will move up the ladder faster,” Mr. Iyer says.

The only exception to this weight given to backroom operators is former Union Minister and current general secretary Smriti Irani, whose oratorical skills have been considered valuable.

The only two general secretaries retained from the older team, Vinod Tawde and Sunil Bansal, have had a good run with Bihar and West Bengal respectively, States they were in charge of. Others such as general secretaries Satish Poonia and Biplab Deb, as well as new vice-president Ram Madhav also have a proven track record of behind-the-scenes organisational work in Jammu and Kashmir, West Bengal and Haryana.

The BJP’s anxieties have more to do with the party’s ability to run the election machinery.

The 2024 Lok Sabha polls and its discontents

The new list of office-bearers hides within it attempts to settle the disquiet engendered by the results of the Lok Sabha poll of 2024, which saw the BJP lose its single-party majority.

The unease between the BJP and its ideological mothership, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), stood out during the 2024 election. It became public when the then BJP president, J.P. Nadda, said during an interview that the party did not require the help of the RSS as electoral muscle, adding that the BJP was “saksham” or adequate for the task.

Long-held resentments within the RSS — of the parent organisation being overlooked while its political wing, the BJP, flexed its muscles — burst to the fore, with particularly harmful effects for the party’s prospects in Maharashtra, where the Mahayuti alliance of the BJP, the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena and the Ajit Pawar-led Nationalist Congress Party suffered electoral losses.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi with BJP national president Nitin Nabin and the party’s newly appointed national office-bearers during an organisational meeting at the BJP headquarters, in New Delhi on August 22. | Photo Credit: ANI

In the Assembly election in the State later that year, this uneasiness was resolved by a coordination mechanism between the BJP and the RSS. The latter was headed by office-bearer Atul Limaye, who helped deliver a win to the alliance.

The awareness that the RSS and the BJP needed each other to remain in power had been reinforced by the results of the Lok Sabha election of 2024.

The return of Mr. Madhav, first as poll in charge of Jammu and Kashmir in the 2024 Assembly election, the first such poll after it became a Union Territory and after the reading down of Article 370 in 2019, and as vice-president in August 2026 was the second part of this rapprochement.

The understanding within the Sangh Parivar that internal issues should not endanger the government was driven home to the RSS and the BJP. Mr. Madhav, in an interview to The Hindu, described himself as someone who believed in a “middle path”. In this case, he was the halfway meeting point for the BJP and RSS.

Analysis: Why Amit Malviya lost his job as BJP’s social media chief 

Insider-outsider

A few months before the BJP announced its new team of national office-bearers, a meeting was held at Defence Minister and former party president Rajnath Singh’s residence.

Those present included not just the new BJP president Nitin Nabin, but also Union Home Minister Amit Shah, party’s general secretary (organisation) B.L. Santhosh, and senior office-bearers of the RSS.

The topic of discussion was how to reconcile the aspirations of old-timers in the party with the flood of newcomers in the BJP since it came to power. This was not a new discussion. In an interview just before the Assembly poll in Assam this year, BJP vice-president and Assam in-charge Baijayant Panda, who was earlier with the Biju Janata Dal, told The Hindu that selectivity in distributing tickets to newcomers was the answer to the conundrum.

The BJP has profited from outside talent, especially since 2014. Three of the party’s Chief Ministers — Himanta Biswa Sarma in Assam, Samrat Choudhary in Bihar and Suvendu Adhikari in West Bengal — have joined the BJP from other political parties.

**EDS: THIRD PARTY IMAGE** In this image posted on Aug. 22, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi speaks during a meeting with newly appointed office-bearers and national functionaries of the party as BJP National President Nitin Nabin and others look on, at BJP Headquarters, in New Delhi. (@narendramodi/X via PTI Photo)(PTI08_22_2026_000557B) | Photo Credit: -

In the new team, Rohan Gupta, who joined the BJP from the Congress, and Sandeep Pathak, who came from the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), have been appointed as national secretaries. They don’t qualify as long-term players within the party, but they do bring in the value of being backroom operators, with Mr. Pathak especially valued for his organisational work for AAP before the Punjab poll of 2022, which AAP had won.

The apprehensions of old-timers in the BJP, who see the party expanding with little reward for themselves, are being soothed by making newcomers do the organisational grind.

All the President’s men

Another issue that arose during the Lok Sabha poll of 2024 was the perception that the organisation’s work was subordinate to that of the government, that the strings of the party were being pulled by a high command, at the cost of the authority of the BJP president.

“Naddaji had been a general secretary in the national team in the past, served an apprenticeship under Amit Shah as the national working president of the BJP in 2019 and his subsequent team gave no inkling of his own personal likes or dislikes,” said a senior office-bearer in the BJP.

BJP national president Nitin Nabin (seen folding his hands) receives a floral welcome upon his arrival to attend the party’s State executive committee meeting, in Haldwani; he is joined by Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami (left). | Photo Credit: PTI

In Mr. Nabin’s case, however, he has had remarkable autonomy in bringing people with whom he shares a good rapport into his team. BJP’s national secretaries Swadesh Singh and Siddharth Shambhu are known to enjoy Nabin’s trust, as does the newly appointed chief of the party’s Scheduled Caste wing, Shivesh Ram.

The new social media cell chief of the party, Deepak Mhaskey from Chhattisgarh, has also been hand-picked by Mr. Nabin, who had worked with him when latter handled the 2023 Assembly poll in that State.

Gen Z protests and social media

It was Mr. Mhaskey’s appointment, replacing long-serving IT cell chief Amit Malviya, that made headlines after the new team was announced. The announcement came on the back of the Gen Z protests against the NEET paper leak, and the pasting that the BJP and the government took on social media throughout that period. That was a departure for a party that had, for the previous 12 years held a tight hold over the narrative, especially on social media.

One reason given for his replacement was the need for the BJP to strategise differently to counter this narrative. At a brainstorming session held soon after the new team’s announcement, with many of its young leaders called in, it was decided not to look at Gen Z as a homogeneous unit. Ami Shah, a political communications professional and visiting faculty member at IIM Bangalore, says that the BJP had hyperlocalised communications in Maharashtra in 2014.

She speaks about having studied the jokes and humour, which were segmented, with people from Vidarbha preferring slapstick humour, while those in Konkan preferred wit.

“The BJP deployed its cultural knowledge of the area effectively in the Assembly poll in Maharashtra in 2014,” she said.

Mr. Mhaskey is supposed to channel these segmented tier-two city and rural sensibilities in the BJP’s communications game, but has had a rough start. Most of his team leaders, Priti Gandhi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav, have had to delete objectionable posts from their social media handles, and some of the content put out by State BJP IT cells and even by the Centre trying to use Gen Z language has turned out to be tone-deaf.

When the new team was announced by the BJP, the party was careful to point out that six of the office-bearers were below the age of 40.

There are 15 between the ages of 40 and 49 and 21 between 50 and 59, bringing the average age of office-bearers to 50 years. More than 40% of the office-bearers come from marginalised communities. Moreover, 12 women from across the country have also made the cut.

The current national team faces the unprecedented challenge of steering the BJP’s efforts to win a fourth term in office in 2029. Apart from the usual distribution of organisational berths to poll-going States, caste groups, and other demographics of gender and age, the new team reflects the BJP’s attempts at a reset as the exigencies of three terms in power kick in.

title: HAL cannot do everything alone, private sector crucial to aerospace ecosystem: CMD Ravi K.
author: Saurabh Trivedi
content_html:
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) cannot develop and manufacture every component on its own and is therefore building a wider domestic aerospace ecosystem by involving private defence manufacturers, including MSMEs and start-ups, HAL Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) Ravi K. said on Thursday (September 17, 2026).

Speaking to The Hindu at the HAL headquarters, Mr. Ravi said the growing number of aerospace programmes and products required greater participation from the private sector.

“HAL cannot do everything on its own. An ecosystem has to be developed because so many products are coming up,” he said, adding that HAL had outsourced major structural components to private vendors while focusing its own resources on core integration and assembly activities. This approach, he said, was aimed at creating a robust domestic supply chain for indigenous aerospace manufacturing.

Comment | Fighter push — integrating HAL’s experience with private enterprise

Tejas frames ready, engines delayed

On the delay in HAL’s deliveries of the light combat aircraft (LCA) Tejas Mk1 to the Indian Air Force (IAF), the HAL CMD said the company was in discussions with GE Aerospace, the original equipment manufacturer (OEM), about delays in engine supplies. “We have 10 engines and we are discussing with the OEM regarding the delays. We are getting the airframe ready so when we get engines, we make the aircraft ready,” he said.

According to Mr. Ravi, HAL currently has 25 Tejas airframes ready. “We are hopeful GE will resolve all their issues and start delivering the balance engines,” he said.

He, however, did not commit to any specific timeline for delivery of the remaining aircraft, saying the process was iterative. “I am not promising any timeline. I have my own internal timeline,” he said.

Awaiting GE proposal

With regard to the GE F414 engine, which is planned to power the LCA Mk2, Mr. Ravi said the ball is in GE’s court. “All technical issues have been resolved. We are expecting the commercial proposal from GE,” he said, noting that GE had earlier indicated it would require around three months to submit the proposal.

“By October, we should get something, or they may take one or two more months since it’s a big project,” Mr. Ravi said.

He added that HAL hopes to receive the Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) clearance from the Ministry of Defence, which will enable the company to proceed towards signing the contract with GE.

HAL has also, for the first time, received dual certification for its Dhruv Next Generation (NG) helicopters, he said, meaning that the company can pursue both military and civil helicopter platforms.

Handover of training aircraft

HAL will hand over the LCA Tejas Final Operational Clearance twin-seater trainer aircraft and HTT-40 basic trainer aircraft to the IAF at an event in Bengaluru on Friday, along with the Dhruv NG helicopters to Pawan Hans Limited.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Civil Aviation Minister K. Rammohan Naidu are scheduled to be present on the occasion, along with stakeholders from the aerospace and defence sectors.

The handover is expected to showcase the expanding capabilities of HAL and its industry partners in designing, developing, and manufacturing aerospace platforms for military as well as civilian applications. It will also highlight the role of the domestic aerospace industry in strengthening indigenous design, development, and manufacturing capabilities, and reducing dependence on foreign sources.

title: 25 years on, Konaseema Railway Line project yet to get on track
author: T. Appala Naidu
content_html:
More than two decades ago, India’s first Dalit Lok Sabha Speaker, G.M.C. Balayogi — son of the Konaseema region — envisioned a 57-km-long Kotipalli–Narsapur railway line. Designed to connect Andhra Pradesh’s rice bowl to Narsapuram railway station via the towns of Amalapuram and Razole, the Konaseema Railway Line promised connectivity and better trade and commerce opportunities.

The ambitious railway line was aligned to pass through the region’s coconut orchards and lush green paddy fields, stretching across the sacred Godavari River’s three mighty branches: the Gouthami, Vynateya, and Vasista.

The project coincided with Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu’s Vision-2020 initiative during his 1999–2004 term. On November 16, 2000, then-Railway Minister Mamata Banerjee laid the foundation stone for the Kotipalli–Narsapur line in Amalapuram town, along with Mr. Balayogi and Mr. Naidu.

For the farmers of the Godavari Delta, the line was supposed to bring affordable transport right to their doorsteps, offering a direct lifeline to market their paddy, coconut, and banana crops.

Yet, nearly twenty-five years later, that promise remains unfulfilled. While construction has progressed in fragmented stretches, persistent hurdles in the form of land acquisition and other obstacles left this crucial project stalled.

For Koripalli Sambasiva, a 70-year-old farmer from Senipalli Lanka village on the banks of Gouthami in Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema district, the hope of one day seeing a train reach Konaseema is still alive. “I am still committed to parting with our family’s ten kunchams of land (one acre) thriving with coconut and banana orchards,” he says.

“Like my fellow farmers 25 years ago, my family and relatives also respected the word of G.M.C. Balayogi and parted with 4.5 acres after his assurance of suitable compensation,” he adds.

The excited farmers parted with their fertile lands, despite it having thrived with crops since the days of British General and Irrigation Engineer Sir Arthur Cotton, who proposed, designed, executed, and completed the construction of the Dowleswaram Anicut on the Godavari River in 1852.

The Konaseema Railway Line, which was progressing efficiently, soon faced its first setback with the sudden death of Mr. Balayogi in a helicopter crash in West Godavari on March 3, 2002.

“After the death of Mr. Balayogi, the erstwhile East Godavari district officials offered ₹2 lakh compensation per acre, which I did not accept. A few years ago, I approached the court for fair compensation, as the government did not initiate talks to reach a consensus,” Mr. Sambasiva says. He was not alone in seeking justice; many farmers from Inavalli Mandal also approached the court with similar appeals. These cases remain in the trial stage.

Former A. Vemavaram Panchayat Sarpanch Daasam Gopala Krishna, farmer Durga Venkata Reddy Naidu, and others from the Amalapuram Rural Mandal have individually approached the Andhra Pradesh High Court for fair compensation and collectively express their desire for the railway line to become a reality.

“Except for fair compensation, none of the farmers oppose the project on any other grounds. We are not strictly demanding the implementation of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation, and Resettlement Act, 2013, in letter and spirit. Any reasonable compensation offer in place of the 2001–02 package is acceptable. However, the government has not proposed any new package to settle the cases,” they say.

Roadblocks

According to officials, the project was planned in three phases: Kotipalli–Amalapuram (12.70 km), Amalapuram–Chinchinada (33.88 km), and Chinchinada–Narsapur (10 km), featuring major bridges across the Gouthami, Vynateya, and Vasista, according to the South Central Railway (SCR) officials. At present, the SCR has completed over 98% of the substructure construction, including bridge pillars.

In some stretches the work has moved ahead, in others, it remains stalled. title: Haripad school launches ‘Vidya Bank’ for hands-on banking lessons
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
In today’s world, children learn about savings and how to manage their money in school. But what if the world of banking is no longer a daunting theoretical lesson and instead becomes an experience that stays with them forever.

At Government Upper Primary School, Vellamkulangara, a rural school near Haripad in Alappuzha district, a student-run temporary bank, named Vidya Bank, has been started by the institution’s Social Science Club to provide students with experiential learning of the banking system.

As a practical extension of the chapter “Let’s Save for the Future” in the Social Science textbook for Class 6 students, V. Rajaneesh, a teacher and the convener of the Social Science Club, along with his students started the experimental banking facility to make students familiar with banking practices and principles.

Vidya Bank operates like a typical bank, with students taking roles such as cashier and manager, handling tasks like account opening and cash management. It functions from a hall on the first floor and is equipped with a bank board and designated counters for its operations..

Forms for opening accounts, KYC updates, deposits and withdrawal have been prepared under the name of Vidya Bank in the same format as found in banks, but with minor tweaks to make it easier for students to fill them in. Even account passbooks have been provided to students.

Accounts can be opened by submitting a copy of the students’ Aadhaar card or two photos and a filled-up KYC form. Teachers help pre-primary and lower primary students with the forms, while upper primary students do it on their own. The accounts can be opened as zero-balance accounts.

All 115 students from pre-primary to class VII and teachers can open accounts and conduct cash transactions on all working days from 9.15 a.m. to 9.45 a.m. and 1.30 p.m. to 2 p.m. at Vidya Bank.

Operations of bank manager, cashier, counters, customer care are handled by Class VII students who learnt about banking in Class VI and can guide the current Class VI students.

The school plans to operate Vidya Bank for three months to help students become familiar with its operations. Students can open fixed deposits for the entirety of that period, in which case an annual interest of 4% is offered to them.

For the convenience of customers, a schedule assigning specific days to different classes for conducting transactions has been prepared.

The formal launch of the bank was held on Wednesday. Grama panchayat president P. Omana and Haripad district educational officer C. Madhu performed the inauguration by handing over the account opening forms to the students. Headmistress P.S. Sindhukumari has provided support to the initiative, besides other staff members and the school’s management and development committees.

Mr. Rajaneesh who has been working at the school for 12 years says the students’ response has been very positive. They are excited about learning about banking and practically handling operations and doing transactions on their own.

title: Charting a smooth path for hosts & guests
author: Rashmi  Patil
content_html:
A home away from home. That is the promise of homestays for tourists travelling from other countries, States, and cities to major tourist destinations in Karnataka. Local families in these accommodations offer tourists a warm and homely atmosphere even as they introduce them to a new culture and guide them to places to visit.

Such accommodations have caught the fancy of tourists in recent years, and according to the Tourism Department officials, there are around 4,000 homestays registered in Karnataka. They are mostly concentrated in Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru, Hassan, Shivamogga in south Karnataka, and Hampi in Vijayanagara district in north Karnataka. These districts attract majority of tourists during monsoon, weekends, and holidays.

However, some untoward incidents in recent times have raised questions about the enforcement of regulations. Most recently, in June 2026, during the hearing of an alleged rape case in a Kodagu homestay, the Karnataka High Court urged the State government and the Tourism Department to frame comprehensive, multisector policies to address safety, compliance, and consumer protection concerns in the hospitality industry.

As per rules, it is mandatory for homestays across the State to register through the online portal of the Tourism Department or the Seva Sindhu Portal under the revised Karnataka Homestay Registration Guidelines, 2025.

Speaking to The Hindu, a senior official from the Tourism Department said that homestays have existed in Karnataka for decades and guidelines were put in place way back in 2006-07. “Since then, the registration of homestays is mandatory. From the past two years, the process has shifted to online portal. However, after some incidents came to light and keeping safety of tourists in mind, we implemented it strictly from June 2026. The department has instructed all district commissioners, in places where homestays come up, to implement the guidelines without fail.”

Unauthorised B&Bs

Despite the guidelines by the department, thousands of unauthorised homestays or Bed & Breakfasts (B&Bs) have come up across tourist destinations in the State. Neither the homestay associations nor the department has an estimate of them, but they agree that such businesses exist.

A Tourism Department official said: “There are only 4,000 authorised or registered homestays. While we don’t have an exact figure of unauthorised homestay, tourists must avoid going to such places.”

Meanwhile, Monthi Ganesh, president, Kodagu Homestay Owners’ Association, said: “At least 2,000 homestays in Kodagu are unauthorised, which means they operate without licence.” She said that people from other States take property on lease and start homestay businesses without following guidelines and procuring licence. “We have complained several times to the police and the district administration, but it hasn’t yielded results.”

The association also goes on inspection of homestays when owners apply for a licence from the department, along with officials. At present, there are more than 2,000 homestays in Kodagu that are registered and around 1,800 of them are affiliated with the association. “The issue of unauthorised homestays came to our notice when we started receiving complaints from tourists of brokers and agents taking them to faraway places for as low as ₹1,000 per person per day.“

The association brought it to the notice of the District Tourism Committee headed by the District Commissioner of Kodagu and other industry veterans during a meeting held on September 11, 2026.

Monthi Ganesh said that every incident of a tourist being cheated, harassed, or ill-treated affects the industry. “Tourists start fearing coming to Kodagu and footfall drops. Authorised homestays are the way forward to tackle these issues.”

Somashekar S.J., District Commissioner, Kodagu, said: “We are aware of unauthorised homestays. The district administration in collaboration with hospitality industry veterans will print a booklet for tourists with a list of authorised homestays, contact numbers, and addresses. Guidelines and emergency helpline numbers will be provided in case of issues during their journey and stay.”

The scenario in Chikkamagaluru is no different. H.L. Giridhar, president of Chikkamagaluru Homestay Owners’ Association, said while around 600 are registered, which includes both homestays and B&B category accommodations, there are over a thousand that are unauthorised and open only on the weekends when the demand from tourists for rooms is high. “The reason behind making registration mandatory is to earn people’s trust and see that when any incidents are reported, the homestay owner is held responsible.”

More transparency needed

Giridhar underlined the need for a transparent process to make this possible. “When I applied for a licence a few years ago, it took three months for the entire process. Another issue is lack of uniformity in the fees charged by the departments for various processes. For instance, panchayats can charge upto ₹500 for issuing NOC though there is no such guideline. However, there are panchayats that charge ₹5,000 to ₹10,000 for issuing NOC (No Objection Certificate), which is not fair. The process of applying and getting a licence should be made easier for owners for the ease of doing business.”

He urged that the government should not encourage proliferation of B&Bs. “It will lead to homestays losing their USP of providing hospitality to guests in the presence of owner on the property. Let the government encourage more owners to run homestays in their own tourist destinations. If you commercialise the idea by allowing non-residents to enter the business, there will be competition forcing homestay owners to charge more in comparison to the existing prices,” he said.

In world heritage site Hampi too, homestays have mushroomed. In August 2026, Justice B. Veerappa, Upalokayukta, visited Hampi and directed officials to clear all unauthorised homestays located within the buffer zone and pheriperal zone of historical monuments and sites.

According to the Upalokayukta, around 250 homestays were flagged as unauthorised. He asked the District Commissioner of Koppal to take legal action against such homestays, disconnect power and water supply services, and submit a detailed report to the Upalokayukta. In his report, he highlighted how agricultural land was also used to build homestays and operate illegally.

In response to this, Dictrict Commissioner Suresh B. Itnal, Koppal district, said the authorities have stopped providing electricity, water, and other facilities to unauthorised homestays. More than 200 such homestays have shut down, he said.

Siraj, homestay owner in Anegundi adjoining Hampi, said: “In 2025, when registration was made mandatory, I tried applying online. The website was not working for almost a year. Finally, in early 2026, I got my homestay registered. Now, one of my friends who runs a homestay has applied for registration, but it has been pending since four months.

The official noted that the department has received over 1,000 applications from homestay owners in the past three to four months, but verification and issuing of licences are pending.

The official explained that homestays need to procure an NOC from gram panchayats, the Revenue Department and a clearance from the Police Department. “These three departments need to have access to one website and work in coordination whenever they go for an inspection. At present, the file moves from one department to the other manually, leading to delays in verification as the department officials are occupied with other daily issues. On the other hand, the gram panchayats have not streamlined this process online. The NOC by panchayats is given manually to owners, which is presented to the police by owners themselves. With such gaps, the process of verifying and issuing licences to homestays gets delayed,” he said.

Sakala website

To address this, the Department of Tourism is planning to bring all three departments on the existing Sakala platform.

The official said: “Whenever a homestay owner applies for a licence, the three departments must be able to upload necessary clarifications, NOC, or even objections. Finally, a district-level officer from the Tourism Department will inspect the homestay. If there are no violations, then the District Commissioner will issue the licence.”

While homestays are under the purview of non-commercial establishments, B&B category accommodations are under the purview of commercial establishments,but the nodal agency to regulate them is the Tourism Department. Recently, Tourism and Energy Minister K.J. George announced that the Karnataka government would introduce stringent regulations and separate frameworks for B&B establishments.

According to the Homestay Registration Guidelines, 2025, B&B category is a privately owned place, including buildings in farms and plantations where the owner of the establishment does not reside but an agent or an operator designated by them resides on the building premises for providing necessary services to visitors.

An official explained that the distinct frameworks for B&B are aimed at preserving the identity of genuine homestays so that it doesn’t hamper the tourism ecosystem, local economy, and business of owners running these homestays. B&B accommodations are at present registered as homestays because they function at homes with multiple rooms.

“Since B&B falls under the category of commercial establishments, they need to apply for land conversion from residence to commercial category, and agriculture to non-agriculture if it is a cultivation land. We are trying to integrate this land conversion process on the Bhoomi portal under the Revenue Department.”

At present, the department is working on various factors to streamline property tax to be levied on B&B properties, which is likely to be same as other commercial properties. The Escoms concerned will verify the electricity meter and the tariff charges will be same as it is for commercial categories. A home away from home. That is the promise of
homestays for tourists
travelling from other countries, States, and cities to major tourist destinations in Karnataka. Local families in these accommodations offer tourists a warm and homely atmosphere even as they introduce them to a new culture and guide them to places to visit.
Such accommodations have caught the fancy of tourists in recent years, and according to the Tourism Department officials, there are around 4,000 homestays registered in Karnataka. They are mostly concentrated in Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru, Hassan, Shivamogga in south Karnataka, and Hampi in Vijayanagara district in north Karnataka. These districts attract majority of tourists during monsoon, weekends, and holidays.
However, some
untoward incidents in recent times
have raised questions about the enforcement of regulations. Most recently, in June 2026, during the hearing of an alleged rape case in a Kodagu homestay, the Karnataka High Court urged the State government and the Tourism Department to frame comprehensive, multisector policies to address safety, compliance, and consumer protection concerns in the hospitality industry.
As per rules, it is mandatory for homestays across the State to register through the online portal of the Tourism Department or the Seva Sindhu Portal under the revised Karnataka Homestay Registration Guidelines, 2025.
Speaking to
The Hindu
, a senior official from the Tourism Department said that
homestays have existed in Karnataka
for decades and guidelines were put in place way back in 2006-07. “Since then, the registration of homestays is mandatory. From the past two years, the process has shifted to online portal. The department has instructed all district commissioners, in places where homestays come up, to implement the guidelines without fail.”

Despite the guidelines by the department, thousands of unauthorised homestays or Bed & Breakfasts (B&Bs) have come up across tourist destinations in the State. Neither the homestay associations nor the department has an estimate of them, but they agree that such businesses exist.
A Tourism Department official said: “There are only 4,000 authorised or registered homestays. While we don’t have an exact figure of unauthorised homestay, tourists must avoid going to such places.”
Meanwhile, Monthi Ganesh, president, Kodagu Homestay Owners’ Association, said: “At least 2,000 homestays in Kodagu are unauthorised, which means they operate without licence.” She said that people from other States take property on lease and start  homestay businesses without following guidelines and procuring licence. “We have complained several times to the police and the district administration, but it hasn’t yielded results.”
The association also goes on inspection of homestays when owners apply for a licence from the department, along with officials. At present, there are more than 2,000 homestays in Kodagu that are registered and around 1,800 of them are affiliated with the association. “The issue of unauthorised homestays came to our notice when we started receiving complaints from tourists of brokers and agents taking them to faraway places for as low as ₹1,000 per person per day.“
The association brought it to the notice of the District Tourism Committee headed by the District Commissioner of Kodagu and other industry veterans during a meeting held on September 11, 2026.
Monthi Ganesh said that every incident of a tourist being cheated, harassed, or ill-treated affects the industry. “Tourists start fearing coming to Kodagu and footfall drops. Authorised homestays are the way forward to tackle these issues.”
Somashekar S.J., District Commissioner, Kodagu, said: “We are aware of unauthorised homestays. The district administration in collaboration with hospitality industry veterans will print a booklet for tourists with a list of authorised homestays, contact numbers, and addresses. Guidelines and emergency helpline numbers will be provided in case of issues during their journey and stay.”
The scenario in Chikkamagaluru is no different. H.L. Giridhar, president of Chikkamagaluru Homestay Owners’ Association, said while around 600 are registered, which includes both homestays and B&B category accommodations, there are over a thousand that are unauthorised and open only on the weekends when the demand from tourists for rooms is high. “The reason behind making registration mandatory is to earn people’s trust and see that when any incidents are reported, the homestay owner is held responsible.”
More transparency needed
Giridhar underlined the need for a transparent process to make this possible. “When I applied for a licence a few years ago, it took three months for the entire process. Another issue is lack of uniformity in the fees charged by the departments for various processes. For instance, panchayats can charge upto ₹500 for issuing NOC though there is no such guideline. However, there are panchayats that charge ₹5,000 to ₹10,000 for issuing NOC (No Objection Certificate), which is not fair. The process of applying and getting a licence should be made easier for owners for the ease of doing business.”
He urged that the government should not encourage proliferation of B&Bs. “It will lead to homestays losing their USP of providing hospitality to guests in the presence of owner on the property. Let the government encourage more owners to run homestays in their own tourist destinations. If you commercialise the idea by allowing non-residents to enter the business, there will be competition forcing homestay owners to charge more in comparison to the existing prices,” he said.
In world heritage site Hampi too, homestays have mushroomed. In August 2026, Justice B. Veerappa, Upalokayukta, visited Hampi and directed officials to clear all unauthorised homestays located within the buffer zone and pheriperal zone of historical monuments and sites.
According to the Upalokayukta, around 250 homestays were flagged as unauthorised. The official noted that the department has received over 1,000 applications from homestay owners in the past three to four months, but verification and issuing of licences are pending.
The official explained that homestays need to procure an NOC from gram panchayats, the Revenue Department and a clearance from the Police Department. “These three departments need to have access to one website and work in coordination whenever they go for an inspection. At present, the file moves from one department to the other manually, leading to delays in verification as the department officials are occupied with other daily issues. On the other hand, the gram panchayats have not streamlined this process online. The NOC by panchayats is given manually to owners, which is presented to the police by owners themselves. With such gaps, the process of verifying and issuing licences to homestays gets delayed,” he said.
Sakala website
To address this, the Department of Tourism is planning to bring all three departments on the existing Sakala platform.
The official said: “Whenever a homestay owner applies for a licence, the three departments must be able to upload necessary clarifications, NOC, or even objections. While homestays are under the purview of non-commercial establishments, B&B category accommodations are under the purview of commercial establishments,

According to the Homestay Registration Guidelines, 2025, B&B category is a privately owned place, including buildings in farms and  plantations where the owner of the establishment does not reside but an agent or an operator designated by them resides on the building premises for providing necessary services to visitors.
An official explained that the distinct frameworks for B&B are aimed at preserving the identity of genuine homestays so that it doesn’t hamper the tourism ecosystem, local economy, and business of owners running these homestays. title: FDA chief Tukaram flags huge price gaps in medical devices, seeks Centre’s intervention
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Munde has initiated action to focus on the drug part of FDA as he has written to the Department of Pharmaceuticals and National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), recommending guidelines on the permissible gap between trade procurement and MRP. 

Calling the gap a core public health issue, Mr. Munde said, “The most expensive part of a hospital bill may never touch the hospital at all. A patient admitted for care has no way of knowing whether the price on a medical consumable reflects its actual cost or a markup fixed long before it ever reached the ward.“ 

Mr. Munde pointed out that the review of the findings of the survey and clear guidelines on the permissible gap between trade procurement price and declared MRP have been recommended to the Department of Pharmaceuticals and the NPPA, and this is not just to close a pricing gap, but also the information gap patients have. 

A survey of hospital consumables in Maharashtra found an IV infusion set with a trade price of ₹11.05 carrying a printed MRP of ₹325, a markup of 2,841%. A syringe procured at ₹6.75 carried an MRP of ₹57.20. A catheter procured at ₹29.41 carried an MRP of ₹310.

Explaining the gap and need for transparency, he said on X that as they are not elective purchases, patients cannot compare prices, seek alternatives, or question the MRP while receiving care. 

“The MRP itself is often fixed upstream by manufacturers and distributors, disconnected from the trade price by a wide, unexplained margin. The result is a system where the party bearing the cost has the least information to evaluate it,” he added. 

The regulatory gap is structural: scheduled medicines are capped under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. Most medical devices and consumables are not covered, leaving both the pricing and the information around it almost entirely unmonitored, he added on X.
